teaser: An 83-year-old with no wig, no teeth and the sharpest smile in Europe.
review_notes:
IMAGE/METADATA MISMATCH: the photo is credited to LACMA (Museum Associates/LACMA) and shows the Los Angeles version of Houdon's Seated Voltaire (a cast, not polished marble), not the 1781 marble in the Comédie-Française named in the catalog. Same composition. The lesson says so in general terms.
Salon of 1781 success: standard account; the description of the public's reaction is kept general, no quotes.
Voltaire returned to Paris in February 1778 after about 28 years away; crowned at the Comédie-Française on 30 March 1778 during Irène; died 30 May 1778 aged 83.
Sittings with Houdon in spring 1778: standard account.
Marble commissioned by Voltaire's niece Madame Denis and given to the Comédie-Française; second marble for Catherine the Great now in the Hermitage.
Pigalle's nude Voltaire (finished 1776, now Louvre) and the mockery it met.
Voltaire's heart kept in the base of Houdon's plaster of this statue at the Bibliothèque nationale de France: please verify wording.
Houdon's trip to Mount Vernon in 1785 to model Washington.
The small shape at the hem read as the tip of a foot (x 0.54, y 0.84) is tiny in the working image: check on the zoom image.
Catalog movement is rococo; the work is usually placed between late Rococo naturalism and Neoclassicism.

lesson.text: Paris, late summer 1781. At the Salon, the big public art show held in the Louvre, the crowd keeps bunching up around one statue. It shows a very old man in an armchair. People stop, grin, and lower their voices, as if he could hear. Several say the same thing: he is about to answer back.

They all knew the face. Voltaire had been the most famous writer in Europe for half a century: plays, histories, pamphlets, thousands of letters, and a talent for mocking kings and priests that got him jailed and then pushed out of Paris for some 28 years. He had died three years before the show, at 83.

When Voltaire finally came back to Paris in 1778, the city went wild. At a performance of his last play at the Comédie-Française, the actors carried his bust on stage and crowned it with laurel while he watched from his box. He died about two months later.

During those last weeks, a 37-year-old sculptor named Jean-Antoine Houdon got him to sit. Houdon was obsessed with accuracy. He measured heads with calipers, studied anatomy on real bodies, and took casts of faces when he could. What he caught in Voltaire, though, cannot be measured.

lesson.title: The head
lesson.text: Everything the first visitors reacted to happens in a few centimeters at the top.

spots.title: Eyes that shine
spots.text: Houdon cut the pupils deep and left a tiny raised point of material inside each. It catches the light like the wet glint of a real eye. The gaze slides sideways, toward someone outside the frame.

spots.title: The smile
spots.text: Thin lips pulled tight over a mouth with no teeth left. The sunken cheeks are not flattered. But the corners turn up: he has thought of a reply and is enjoying it in advance.

spots.title: No wig
spots.text: A gentleman of his time would be shown in a powdered wig. Voltaire has his own thin hair, tied with a plain band like the ones on ancient busts of philosophers and poets.

lesson.text: Houdon's portraits show a mind at work. He keeps every wrinkle, then adds the one thing a cast of a face cannot give: a passing thought.

The body was a harder problem. How do you dress a hero of ideas? In modern clothes he would look like any old gentleman in a coat. As an ancient Roman in a toga he would look like a costume party. And one sculptor had already tried a third way, with painful results.

A few years earlier, Jean-Baptiste Pigalle had carved Voltaire completely naked, in the manner of ancient heroes, with the true body of a man in his late seventies. Paris laughed so hard that the statue was kept out of public view for years. It is in the Louvre today.

Houdon's answer is a big loose robe that belongs to no period. It could be the dressing gown the old man really wore at his desk, or the cloak of a Greek thinker. It hides the frail body and lets Houdon build a calm mountain of folds, from which a head and two hands stick out.

spots.title: The gripping hand
spots.text: Bony fingers close over the arm of the chair. Tendons and knuckles stand out. The face is amused, but this hand is tense, as if he were about to push himself up.

spots.title: The other hand
spots.text: It hooks over the front of the far armrest. Both arms are braced, and the whole upper body tips forward and turns. This is someone leaning into a conversation.

spots.title: The armchair
spots.text: The arm rests on a little turned post, and the legs are grooved like small columns. It is a chair in the newest taste of the 1770s, inspired by ancient furniture.

spots.title: A mountain of folds
spots.text: From knees to floor the robe drops in long, heavy pleats. There is no pattern, no lace, no button. The plainness sends your eye back up to the face.

spots.title: At the hem
spots.text: Where the cloth pools on the base, a small shape pokes out from under the edge: the tip of a foot. It is the only hint that there are legs under all this fabric.

lesson.text: The lean, the grip and the sideways look add up to one story: he is listening to somebody and is half a second from cutting in. That is what the Salon crowd felt. Houdon gave a seated statue of a dead man the suspense of a dinner table.

The first marble was ordered by Voltaire's niece, who gave it to the Comédie-Française, the Paris theater where his plays were staged. Catherine the Great of Russia, his pen friend for years, wanted her own, now in St. Petersburg. The workshop also produced casts. The one in this photo is a cast, with a matte, mottled surface in place of polished marble.
Voltaire's heart was removed after his death and kept by admirers. It ended up in the national library of France, sealed inside the base of Houdon's own plaster of this seated statue.

The Voltaire made Houdon the portraitist every great name wanted. Benjamin Franklin and Thomas Jefferson sat for him in Paris. In 1785 he crossed the Atlantic and stayed at Mount Vernon to take a mold of George Washington's face. If you can picture these men at all, you are probably picturing a Houdon.

quiz.question: When did Houdon study Voltaire from life?
options: In the last weeks of Voltaire's life, in 1778
Never, he worked only from paintings
quiz.explanation: Voltaire sat for him shortly before dying at 83.

quiz.question: How did Houdon make the eyes seem alive?
options: He set glass beads in them
He left a tiny raised point inside each deep-cut pupil
quiz.explanation: The small point catches light like the glint of a real eye.

quiz.question: What went wrong with Pigalle's earlier statue of Voltaire?
options: It showed the old man naked and was mocked
quiz.explanation: Pigalle carved him nude like an ancient hero, and Paris laughed.

quiz.question: Why did Houdon choose a loose, timeless robe?
options: It was the uniform of French writers
It avoided both everyday dress and a Roman costume
Voltaire had demanded it in his will
quiz.explanation: The robe belongs to no period and hides the frail body.

quiz.question: Which American did Houdon travel to Mount Vernon to portray?
quiz.explanation: He crossed the Atlantic in 1785 to model Washington.

facts.text: Voltaire is shown wearing a powdered wig.
facts.explanation: He has his own thin hair, tied with a plain band.

facts.text: A marble version was made for Catherine the Great of Russia.
facts.explanation: She had corresponded with Voltaire and wanted her own statue.

facts.text: Voltaire's hands lie relaxed in his lap.
facts.explanation: Both hands grip the arms of the chair as if he were about to rise.
